title: How Airports Make Money (It's Not the Planes)

beats.say: Airports make huge amounts of money from people who aren't flying anywhere at all. And from the people who are, they make it long before they get on the plane.

Think about the last time you went to an airport. You probably paid to park, or paid to drop someone off. You queued through security. And then, before you could reach your gate, you were walked straight through a giant shop.

vis.title: Your trip through an airport
items: Pay to park or drop off

beats.say: None of that is an accident. Let's follow the money, from the car park to the gate.

vis.text: Let's follow the money, car park to gate.

beats.say: Part one. Two kinds of money.

An airport earns money in two ways. Aeronautical money comes from airlines. Landing fees, parking for planes, and charges for every passenger. Commercial money comes from everything else. Shops, restaurants, car parks, advertising and property.
The fees charged to airlines are often limited by regulators, or squeezed down by tough airlines like Ryanair. But the money from shops, food and parking is where airports can really grow.
Part two. The car park.

Car parking is one of the most profitable things an airport does. Once the car park is built, each extra car costs almost nothing. And people flying abroad will often pay a lot to avoid missing their flight.

vis.sub: Built once, paid for every day

beats.say: Many airports now even charge you for dropping someone off outside the terminal, often several pounds for just a few minutes. A few minutes of tarmac, paid for by thousands of cars every day.

vis.title: What a few minutes can cost (illustrative)
vis.source: Illustrative examples; prices vary by airport

beats.say: And the pricing is clever. Turn up without booking, and parking can be very expensive. Book weeks ahead online, and it's cheaper. Airports use this to fill their car parks, and to make the most from people in a rush.
Part three. The walk-through shop.

As soon as you clear security, many airports send you straight into a winding shop full of perfume, alcohol and chocolate. There's often no way around it. The only path to your gate goes through the shop.

vis.title: The only way to your gate

beats.say: It works because of timing. You've just been through the most stressful part of the trip. Now you're relaxed, you're early, and you're in holiday mode. That's exactly when people spend.

vis.text: Relaxed, early and in holiday mode.

beats.say: At Heathrow, retail and other commercial income came to about seven hundred and ninety one million pounds in twenty twenty five. That worked out at roughly nine pounds thirty six for every single passenger.

vis.label: retail revenue per Heathrow passenger in 2025
vis.source: Heathrow 2025 results, reported by Moodie Davitt (retail revenue £791m, 84.5m passengers)

beats.say: With eighty four and a half million passengers a year, even a few pounds each adds up to an enormous amount.

Airports also study how people move. They know that the longer you spend airside, the more you spend. That's why gates are often announced late, keeping you in the main shopping area until the last moment instead of sitting at the gate.
Part four. Why food costs more airside.

Ever wondered why a sandwich costs more after security? It's not only greed. Airports charge restaurants and shops high rents, often a share of everything they sell. Staff need security checks. Deliveries have to be screened. All of that pushes prices up.

vis.title: Why airside costs more
items: High rents, often a share of sales

beats.say: And once you're airside, you can't easily nip out to a cheaper shop. You're a captive audience.

vis.text: Once you're airside, you're a captive audience.

beats.say: That's why many airports promise to price some things the same as the high street, like bottled water. It stops passengers feeling ripped off, while everything else carries the airport premium.
Part five. Duty free, and who really saves.

Duty free sounds like a guaranteed bargain. But for flights within Europe, the rules are different, and some products aren't actually cheaper than in a supermarket. Retailers sometimes set their own prices well above what you'd pay online.
The tip is simple. Look up the price on your phone before you buy. Duty free can be a good deal, but it isn't always.
Part six. Ads, lounges and land.

Airports also sell advertising space to brands that want to reach travellers with money to spend. They charge for fast-track security and lounges. They rent out land for hotels, offices and warehouses. Some even earn from money exchange desks.

Some of the busiest airports are owned by investment funds and pension funds. They love airports for the same reason they love toll roads. People will always need to travel, and there's usually no competitor next door.

vis.text: Investors love airports like toll roads.

beats.say: So how do you avoid paying the airport premium? Book parking early, or get the train. Bring an empty water bottle and fill it after security. Eat before you go. And check duty free prices on your phone.
Because to an airport, you're not just a passenger. You're a shopper who happens to be catching a plane.

vis.text: You're a shopper who happens to catch a plane.

beats.say: Subscribe for more on how the places you visit really make their money. And tell me in the comments the most you've ever paid for something at an airport.
